sections.name: The vine's year
sections.source: New Mexico State University Extension, Grapevine Phenology (Guide H-338)

lines.label: Two cycles
lines.text: Shoots grow in one season, but fruit takes two: buds formed this year carry next year's clusters.

lines.label: Light and heat
lines.text: Day length sets dormancy, flowering and ripening; heat speeds them up. Heat is counted as growing degree days above 50°F.

know: The modified E-L scale numbers the stages: budburst 4, flowering 23, fruit set 27, veraison 35, harvest 38.
Flowering usually starts when temperatures reach about 68°F.
Fruit set counts as good if about one flower in three becomes a berry.
At veraison berries soften, change color and start building sugar.
Sparkling-wine grapes are picked around 14–18° Brix; table-wine grapes usually at 21–24°.

sections.name: Training and the canopy
sections.source: Wine Folly; University of Minnesota Extension; University of New Hampshire Extension; New Mexico State University Extension; Frontiers in Plant Science (2020)

lines.label: Cane or spur
lines.text: Cane pruning lays down one or two fresh canes each winter. Spur pruning keeps a permanent cordon and cuts last year's growth back to short spurs.

lines.label: The canopy
lines.text: The canopy is the vine's leaves. Training and canopy work decide how much sun and air reach the fruit.

know: Cane pruning (Guyot) is common in cooler places such as Burgundy, Sonoma and Oregon.
Spur pruning (cordon) is common in warmer places such as California, Washington and Spain.
A spur is a cane cut back to one to three buds.
VSP trains shoots upright with a low fruit zone, around 3.5–4 feet.
Scott Henry splits the canopy: upper shoots trained up, lower shoots down.

lines.label: Organic in the US
lines.text: Two certified label categories: 'organic' and 'made with organic grapes'. The difference is mostly added sulfites and the USDA seal.

lines.label: Biodynamic
lines.text: Demeter certification starts from organic, then treats the farm as one living, self-sustaining organism, with nine preparations numbered 500 to 508.

know: 'Organic' wine: certified organic grapes, no added sulfites, USDA organic seal allowed.
'Made with organic grapes': all grapes organic, sulfur dioxide up to 100 ppm, no USDA seal.
A wine mixing organic and non-organic grapes can only say 'organic' in its ingredient list.
Demeter farms must set aside at least 10% of their land as a biodiversity reserve.
Preparations 500 (horn manure) and 501 (horn silica) go on every harvested crop at least once a year.

sections.name: Fermentation choices
sections.source: Australian Wine Research Institute (carbonic maceration, whole-bunch, MLF and amber wine); OIV resolution OIV-ECO 647-2020

lines.label: Reds
lines.text: Whole clusters and carbonic maceration both keep bunches intact, but only carbonic seals them under carbon dioxide before any juice runs.

lines.label: Whites
lines.text: MLF softens acid and can add butter. Long skin contact turns a white amber and gives it tannin.

know: Whole-cluster: intact bunches go in the fermenter, usually under destemmed fruit, and get crushed as it goes.
Carbonic maceration: intact bunches, no free juice, in a closed vessel full of carbon dioxide.
Under carbonic, fermentation starts inside the whole berry, without yeast; yeast finishes the job after crushing.
MLF is done mainly by Oenococcus oeni, turning malic acid into lactic acid.
The OIV's 'white wine with maceration' needs white grapes and at least a month on the skins.

lines.label: Species
lines.text: French and Eastern European barrels use Quercus robur or Quercus petraea. American barrels use Quercus alba.

lines.label: New or used
lines.text: New barrels give more flavor and more oxygen. After about four uses a toasted barrel is neutral: it holds wine but adds no flavor.

know: French oak gives subtler aromas and a silky texture; American oak is more assertive, with sweet vanilla.
American oak has two to three times the methyl-octalactone (whisky lactone, coconut) of European oak.
European oak gives almost twice the ellagic tannins of American oak, so the wine is more tannic.
Eastern European oak is the same species as French and tastes much like it.
Tight grain releases more aroma; open grain gives more tannin.

facts.fact: Advanced theory topics: Viticulture (vine cycle, factors of production, vine-training systems, cause and effect in the vineyard, types of viticulture: organic/biodynamic) and Vinification (techniques, cause and effect in the winery, all types of winemaking). Areas of Study list winery items including fermentation techniques, oak usage and type, malolactic fermentation and carbonic maceration.
Grapevine phenology has a vegetative cycle (one season) and a reproductive cycle (two seasons): buds formed in year one give rise to shoots carrying fruit in year two.
Bud dormancy, flowering, fruit ripening, leaf senescence and cold acclimation are set by day length; temperature drives and can accelerate growth. Growing degree days accumulate above a 50°F base.
Modified E-L stages: E-L 1 dormancy, E-L 4 budburst, E-L 23 flowering, E-L 27 fruit set, E-L 35 veraison, E-L 38 harvest, E-L 43 beginning of leaf fall.
Shoot growth is slow in cool early spring, then rapid (10-12 inches per week) in the grand period of growth.

Bloom typically occurs when temperatures reach about 68°F. Up to 1,000 flowers per cluster; berry set is successful if one in three flowers becomes a berry. Cool, cloudy conditions at bloom can cut bud fruitfulness.

Veraison (E-L 35) is berry softening, color change and increasing sugar. Sparkling-wine grapes are harvested around 14-18° Brix; table wines usually 21-24° Brix. After harvest, leaves keep building reserves before dormancy.

Lateral shoot leaves can be 20-50% of total leaf area; excessive laterals shade the canopy and restrict airflow, which can raise disease pressure and lower berry quality. Leaf removal, hedging and shoot thinning/positioning are canopy management.

Cane pruning (Guyot) is commonly used in cooler regions including Burgundy, Sonoma and Oregon; spur pruning (cordon) in warmer regions including California, Washington and Spain. Spurs are short stubs of one to three buds. Goblet training suits drought-prone areas.
A spur is a cane pruned to 1-3 buds; a cordon is a semi-permanent branch off the trunk. Cane-pruned systems are often better in cold areas because they are less susceptible to winter injury.

VSP is an upright system with the fruiting zone around 3.5-4 feet. Scott Henry is a vertically split double canopy (upper canopy up, lower canopy down) that can decrease vine vigor. Geneva Double Curtain uses a bilateral cordon on each side and helps reduce vigor and increase yields.

Methoxypyrazines contribute herbaceous characteristics; IBMP drives bell pepper character. In a Cabernet Sauvignon trial, leaf removal, shoot thinning and both together decreased IBMP from mid-ripening to harvest; prior work found IBMP decreased with greater solar exposure from canopy management.

USDA organic wine labeling (Feb 2014): 'Organic' wine needs certified organic grapes, organic yeast unless unavailable, no added sulfites (only naturally occurring, under 10 ppm), and may use the USDA organic seal. 'Made with organic grapes': all grapes certified organic, sulfur dioxide up to 100 ppm declared on the label, no USDA seal, other agricultural ingredients such as yeast needn't be organic. Both are overseen by a certifier, and labels go through TTB's COLA approval. Wine with organic and non-organic grapes can only make organic claims in the ingredient statement.
Biodynamics derives from Rudolf Steiner's 1924 Agricultural Course, which presented the farm as a living, self-contained, self-sustaining organism; Demeter was formed in 1928 to codify it.
To qualify for Demeter Biodynamic certification a farm must first meet NOP organic requirements; some NOP-permitted inputs are further restricted.
A Demeter farm must keep at least 10% of its total effective land base as a biodiversity reserve.

Nine preparations numbered 500-508, made from herbs, minerals and manures, used in field sprays and compost in tiny doses; their use is required. 500 and 501 must be applied at least annually to all harvested crops: 500 later in the day as droplets on the earth, 501 early morning as a fine mist on foliage.

Appendix J: 500 is cow manure packed in a cow horn, buried over winter; 501 is ground quartz/silica in a horn, buried over summer; 502 yarrow, 503 chamomile, 504 stinging nettle, 505 oak bark, 506 dandelion, 507 valerian; 508 is Equisetum (horsetail), made as a tea.

Whole-bunch fermentation places intact bunches in the fermenter, usually with destemmed/crushed berries on top, crushed by plunging or foot-treading as fermentation goes. Stems can add cut-grass and herbal aromas, possibly higher pH and lower acidity, and more tannin; overdone, it gives astringency and greenness. Effect on color is unclear.

Carbonic maceration: 100% intact bunches with no free juice in a closed vessel filled with CO2, for around a week, then destemmed, crushed and fermented with yeast. Intracellular fermentation inside the intact berry turns some sugar and malic acid into ethanol without yeast.

Carbonic maceration is common with Gamay, Pinot Noir and Shiraz for light-bodied, brightly colored, perfumed or fruity wines for early drinking, with strawberry/raspberry and cherry/kirsch notes. Spoilage risk (acetic bacteria, Brettanomyces) rises.

MLF converts L-malic acid to L-lactic acid, mainly by Oenococcus oeni; it is done in virtually all reds, numerous whites and sparkling bases. It reduces acidity, stabilizes wine and shapes aroma. Diacetyl from MLF gives buttery/butterscotch aroma. Longer MLF raises diacetyl; higher bacteria numbers and long lees contact lower it; co-inoculation with yeast gives fruitier, less buttery wines.

OIV 'white wine with maceration' (OIV-ECO 647-2020): only white grape varieties, fermented with prolonged contact with pomace, maceration of at least one month; can show an orange-amber color and a tannic taste.

Amber or orange wines are white grapes made with red-winemaking techniques; skin contact extracts aroma and phenolics, adding texture and savory complexity; the wine is typically orange at the end of fermentation; tannin is less retained than in reds.

French oak is Quercus robur or Q. petraea (forests include Allier, Limousin, Nevers, Tronçais, Vosges): subtler aromatics, silky texture, tighter grain. American oak is Quercus alba: more assertive, sweeter vanillin-based compounds, looser grain. Eastern European oak (Romania, Hungary, Slovenia) is the same species as French, with similar aromas and firm tannin.

Super-fine grain releases more aromatics; open grain gives more tannin. Older trees and trees from cooler climates grow tighter grain. Staves are seasoned outdoors at least two years. Vanillin is released at all toast levels. Toasted barrels can be used about four times before they are considered neutral.

American oak is more aggressive with more vanillin; French oak has more tannin with less obvious oaky flavor. Fermenting in oak and lees contact with stirring (bâtonnage) make woody character less pronounced and better integrated. Oak descriptors include coconut, vanilla, roasted, smoky and spicy.

European oak gives almost twice the ellagic tannins of American oak; American oak is two to three times richer in methyl-octalactone. New barrels give much more oxygen than used. Untoasted wood supplies whisky lactone (coconut); toasting increases vanilla, toffee and sweet elements; moderate toast brings out spice; heavy toast gives espresso notes and richness. MLF is believed to increase release of oak aroma compounds.
At the Advanced tasting exam, describe a compound's aroma or flavor (green pepper, or green pepper from pyrazines), not just its name.

unverified: Demeter's wine processing rules (native yeast, sulfite limits for 'Biodynamic wine' versus 'made with Biodynamic grapes') could not be read from Demeter's own standard; secondary sources disagree (100 ppm versus 70/90 mg/L). Left out.

Toasting and oak lactone: Virginia Tech says lactone levels rise with seasoning and toasting; a UC Davis lab page and a Cornell study (search summaries only) say heavier toast lowers them. The lesson only says untoasted wood supplies whisky lactone.
Barrel sizes (Bordeaux barrique 225 L, Burgundy pièce 228 L) were found only on secondary sites, not on an official or academic page I could read. Left out.
The USDA organic wine labeling guide read is dated February 2014; it was not checked against the current eCFR text.
The planting calendar often linked with biodynamics is not in the Demeter Farm Standard read. Left out.

The methoxypyrazine study is one Cabernet Sauvignon vineyard in one season; its authors tie the drop more to leaf-to-fruit balance than to sunlight alone. The lesson says canopy work lowered methoxypyrazines and that prior work linked this to sun exposure.
Wine Folly's regional examples for cane and spur pruning are generalizations; many regions use both.
The Demeter standard PDF is filed as 2026 but its cover reads March 2023.
The grapes.extension.org annual-cycle page could not be reached; the vine cycle follows NMSU Guide H-338 instead.

stops.name: Species
stops.text: **American** oak has two to three times the **methyl-octalactone** (whisky lactone: coconut, vanilla). **European** oak gives almost twice the **ellagic tannins**, so a firmer wine.

stops.name: Grain
stops.text: **Tight grain** releases more aroma. **Open grain** gives more tannin. Old trees from cool forests give the tightest grain.

stops.name: Toast
stops.text: Untoasted wood gives **coconut**. Toasting adds **vanilla** and **toffee**, moderate toast brings **spice**, heavy toast gives **espresso**.

stops.name: New or used
stops.text: **New** barrels give more flavor and far more **oxygen**. After about **four uses** a toasted barrel is **neutral**. Fermenting in oak and stirring the **lees** fold the wood in more gently.

read.mixup: **American** oak is the coconut-and-vanilla one. **French** oak is subtler but more tannic.
read.sayIt: French oak, so the wood is in the background and the fruit leads.

diacetyl from malolactic fermentation.
and sweet vanilla point to American oak.

not just the compound: 'green pepper', not 'pyrazines'.

read.bigIdea: Every clue in the glass has a cause.
read.where: The Court's theory guide keeps returning to **cause and effect**. Put this chapter to work by reading backward: from the **clue** to the **cause**, then to the likely grape and place.

stops.name: Green pepper
stops.text: **Methoxypyrazines** give herbal, bell pepper notes. Canopy work like **leaf removal** and **shoot thinning** lowered them in Cabernet Sauvignon berries.

stops.name: Butter
stops.text: **Diacetyl** from **MLF**. A long, slow MLF tends to leave more of it.

stops.name: Coconut and vanilla
stops.text: **American oak**. Espresso points to a **heavy toast**.

stops.name: Kirsch and stems
stops.text: Bright **kirsch** and **strawberry** in a light red can mean **carbonic**. Herbal notes with firmer tannin can mean **whole clusters**.

stops.name: On exam day
stops.text: Describe the smell first. **'Green pepper'** or **'green pepper from pyrazines'** works; **'pyrazines'** alone doesn't.

read.mixup: **Diacetyl** (butter) comes from MLF. **Whisky lactone** (coconut) comes from oak.
read.sayIt: That hint of butter comes from a second, softening fermentation.
